claims.text: Introducing a controlled three-dimensional twin network into fusion plasma-facing FCC alloys will enhance high-temperature plastic strain and toughness.
Twin-induced strain hardening impedes dislocation glide while facilitating distributed plasticity.
The starting material is a conventional single-phase FCC alloy suitable for plasma-facing components and lacks an engineered twin network.
Spark plasma sintering combined with tailored thermomechanical treatment can induce and control a three-dimensional hierarchical twin network in the grains.
The hypothesized twin-network effect operates during deformation at 600–1000 °C.
A three-dimensional hierarchical twin network acts as a substantial barrier to dislocation motion.
The twin network increases strain hardening.
Twin-boundary interfaces provide alternate pathways for dislocation slip and thereby permit substantial plastic deformation.
The combined barrier and slip-pathway roles of the twin network delay plastic instability.
The combined barrier and slip-pathway roles of the twin network enhance toughness at high temperature.
Relative to the baseline, the twin-engineered material will have a higher strain-hardening rate.
Relative to the baseline, the twin-engineered material will sustain more plastic strain before failure.
Relative to the baseline, the twin-engineered material will exhibit improved fracture toughness.
The mechanism should apply broadly to FCC high-temperature structural alloys typical of fusion plasma-facing components.
The magnitude of the effect depends on alloy composition, processing parameters, and operating conditions.
The interaction between irradiation or other plasma-facing environments and the twin network is uncertain.
CrCoNi has a high calculated twinnability, and this twinning propensity is associated with its strength, ductility, and toughness.
Hot plastic deformation in CoCrFeMnNi has activation energies close to weighted diffusion activation energy.
